description: Soy Jarol Nicolás, estudiante de octavo semestre de Ingeniería Electrónica en la Universidad Industrial de Santander (UIS). Mi formación abarca Deep Learning, diseño de circuitos integrados, electrónica, automatización, control y procesamiento de señales, además de dibujo técnico. Me interesa aplicar estas áreas en proyectos que combinen hardware, análisis de datos y sistemas inteligentes.
summary: Tolima burns every year, but understanding when and where is not simple: the NASA satellites that watch for fire, MODIS since 2000 and VIIRS since 2012, see it through different eyes. We created an interactive burning calendar that brings their observations together into one 26-year story. To do this we harmonized the data in time, comparing what both sensors saw in the same periods and may be the same fire, and in space, gathering nearby hotspots that belong to the same event. Anyone, from children to researchers and professionals, can now explore, from their phone, the burning seasons, the most critical years and their link with El Niño, see each fire on the map and compare images from before and after it. Sati, a small guide satellite with a voice, walks users through the journey so the information is clear for everyone, not only specialists. We want firefighters, environmental authorities and communities to have a simple tool to get ahead of the dry seasons and care for their land.
details:
• What does it do?

It is a website that works on a phone or computer and tells the story of fire in Tolima. It has a calendar showing, month by month or week by week, how much fire there was and whether that period was normal or unusual; a map with every hotspot and the grouped fires, with their date, duration, intensity and the type of land where they happened; a slider to compare satellite images before and after a fire; and background maps that change by year and by season since 2000. It also explains which hot spots are not wildfires, such as the Nevado del Ruiz volcano or some industries, and features Sati, a guide who narrates what you discover.

  • How does it work? 

We started from NASA’s hotspot records (FIRMS) and, through the DANE website, attached the outline map of Tolima’s municipalities to place each hotspot in its municipality. Then we set aside what is not vegetation fire, such as the volcano and industrial heat sources. Next we harmonized both sensors: in time, comparing MODIS and VIIRS observations from the same period that may represent the same fire, to bring all 26 years to a common scale; and in space, grouping nearby hotspots that correspond to the same event. With that series we learned what is normal for each time of year, which lets us highlight unusual periods. Finally we added Landsat and Sentinel-2 images processed in Google Earth Engine to show the landscape of each season and the burned areas, and published everything as an open website.

  •  What benefits does it have?

It compares 26 years fairly, without the satellite change looking like more fire. It is free, open and can be taken to any region. It tells wildfires apart from other heat sources, connects each fire with real before-and-after images, and it is visual and voice-guided, designed for anyone to use from their phone.

  •  What is the intended impact of the project?

We want children, young people, adults, professionals, fire departments, CORTOLIMA, disaster risk management agencies, local governments, and communities across Tolima, regardless of their age or level of knowledge, to better understand when and where Tolima burns, so they can prepare before the dry seasons and El Niño years. We also want young girls and boys to connect with these topics from an early age: the website includes an interactive animated video that explains, step by step and in Sati's voice, how satellites detect fire, designed for both children and adults. Next, we would like to send alerts when a week has more fire than normal and bring the tool to other regions of Colombia and the world.

  • What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

Languages: JavaScript, HTML/CSS, Python. Web: Leaflet 1.9.4, SVG/Canvas, GitHub Pages. Data processing: pandas, Pillow, NumPy-style analysis, Google Earth Engine (earthengine-api), NASA GIBS WMTS, NASA FIRMS API. Voice: edge-tts (Microsoft neural voice). Tools: Git/GitHub, Miniconda, Microsoft Edge (headless testing). Hardware: a personal laptop; no special hardware.

  • How is your project creative?

Instead of another technical dashboard, we turned 26 years of satellite data into a story anyone can follow. Sati, a small guide satellite with its own voice, welcomes users, explains what they are seeing and shares curious facts about each year, municipality or fire. An interactive animated video shows, step by step, how satellites detect fire from space, so children and adults can understand it together. We also brought two different satellites into one single calendar, letting people travel through time: pick a year or a season, watch the landscape change on the map, and slide between images taken before and after a fire to see the burn scar appear. Even the "false fires" become a learning moment, with friendly icons that reveal a volcano, a cement kiln or a rice mill and explain why they glow from space.

  • What factors did your team consider?

We thought first about the people who will use it: firefighters, environmental authorities, municipalities, teachers, families and children, many of whom access the internet only from a phone. That is why the site is free, light, works on mobile and is guided by voice and simple language. We cared about trust: the data come from NASA and other official sources, the results were compared with a study from the University of Tolima, and we removed heat sources that are not wildfires so the map does not cause false alarms. We considered the local reality of Tolima, with its two dry seasons and the influence of El Niño, and the frequent cloud cover that limits satellite images. We also considered openness and reuse, so any region can adapt the tool, and transparency, clearly marking where AI tools helped us.
